“Putting a stop to American workers, farmers, and businesses being ripped off by lopsided trade agreements has been a key foundation of President Trump’s Make America Great Again movement,” said White House spokesman Matthew Middleton, adding that the administration would “continue fighting to lower costs”.

Tariffs also have brought a new revenue source to the federal government after Trump’s signature 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act cemented lower individual tax rates.

Trump’s protectionist policies have drawn support from some blue-collar labor groups that historically backed Democrats, even as some Republicans recoil from an economic tool they view as hostile to free markets.

United Steelworkers International President Roxanne Brown on Wednesday called the administration’s actions “long overdue”. The group endorsed Trump’s Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris, in 2024.

Republican US Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska, a Trump critic who is retiring from Congress, took a different view. Calling tariffs “a tax on American consumers” and blaming high inflation and lower wage growth for Republicans’ losses, he urged lawmakers to reclaim authority over import duties. REUTERS

news.title: Gavin Newsom to Face Uphill Battle in Possible 2028 Run, Top Democrat Strategist Predicts — as Cali Gov. Will Have to 'Overcome' Major 'Problem'
news.text:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville warned that California Gov. Gavin Newsom could face a significant obstacle if he seeks the presidency in 2028, arguing that voters may be reluctant to support a candidate so closely associated with the state's liberal politics, RadarOnline.com has learned.

Carville said Newsom would need to address concerns about his political identity.

"He's got to overcome that kind of barrier," Carville warned, arguing that an "uber coastal candidate" might not appeal to voters looking for a different direction.Gavin Newsom's Political SkillsDespite those concerns, both strategists acknowledged Newsom's political abilities.

McKinnon said he once considered Newsom "a little too slick, a little too Hollywood," but came away impressed by his ability to communicate and defend his positions.

"I mean, he's got chops," McKinnon said. Carville agreed that Newsom possesses considerable political experience.

"To his credit, he's a real California guy," Carville said. "He don't try to fake it."Gavin Newsom's Political IdentityDemocratic strategist Doug Schoen raised separate concerns about Newsom's consistency, telling Fox News that the governor has struggled to establish a clear national political identity.

"Gavin Newsom has no clear identity," Schoen said. "His strengths are that he's telegenic, quick on his feet and engaging."

Newsom has defended his administration's record, saying California had delivered policies Democrats support across a range of issues.

California has expanded paid sick leave, provided universal free school meals and enacted abortion protections under Newsom, while critics have pointed to the state's high housing costs, taxes and homelessness problems.Gavin Newsom Sets January TimelineNewsom recently provided a timeline for deciding whether to enter the 2028 race. His term as California governor ends in January 2027, when Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra takes office.

news.title: Maine Democrat Senator-Elect Troy Jackson Backs Chris Van Hollen to Oust Chuck Schumer as Majority Leader
news.text:
Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-ME), a longtime skeptic of Senate Democrat Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY), announced Wednesday that he will vote for Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) in the upcoming Senate Democrat leadership election, citing their shared support for eliminating the filibuster, passing Medicare for All, and increasing the minimum wage.

Jackson, who defeated longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) in the November midterm elections, announced his decision in a November 25 statement ahead of the December 1 secret ballot to determine who will lead Democrats’ incoming 56-seat Senate majority.

“I’ve talked with Mainers about what they need from the Senate, and I believe it’s time for a change in leadership. I’ll be voting for Senator Van Hollen. When we spoke, I told him Maine needs a seat at the table when the caucus decides what gets funded and what we’re going to fight for. I was impressed by his vision for the caucus, and I came away confident he’ll take Maine’s priorities seriously,” Jackson stated.

“From one end of Maine to the other, I heard the same thing. People are working harder, falling further behind, and getting tired of being told to wait. Senator Van Hollen and I agree that it’s time to end the filibuster, pass Medicare for All, and give working people a raise by increasing the minimum wage. I want a leader who’ll bring those fights to the floor,” he continued.

“Mainers voted for change in November, and they ought to get it. Whoever leads this caucus, I’ll fight like hell to make sure the Senate takes on the problems Mainers sent me to Washington to solve,” Jackson concluded.

Jackson’s endorsement comes as an Economist/YouGov poll conducted November 20–23 found that Democrats surveyed preferred Van Hollen over Schumer by 21 percentage points, 40 percent to 19 percent, while 2024 Kamala Harris voters surveyed favored the Maryland Democrat by 30 points, 48 percent to 18 percent. During a Sunday appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, Van Hollen expressed confidence that he could secure the 28 votes needed to defeat Schumer, citing the endorsement of Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI). “We’re north of 15 and momentum is in our direction,” he said. During a November 15 appearance on ABC’s This Week, Van Hollen accused Schumer’s team of spreading “misinformation” and “trying to instill fear in people who may say that they’re going to support me as a new leader.”

Approximately 35 Hollywood figures, including Jane Fonda and Robert De Niro, have also signed a letter urging Senate Democrats to replace Schumer, according to a New York Times report covered by Breitbart News Tuesday. Comedian Jon Stewart and Marvel actor Mark Ruffalo have notably advocated a leadership change. Ruffalo subsequently faced accusations of antisemitism after calling for leadership that followed “the will of the people not entrenched religious beliefs and loyalties,” defending his remarks by citing Schumer’s 2018 AIPAC speech and calling for the consistent enforcement of domestic and international law.

Jackson, a former Maine Senate president and majority leader, defeated Collins in the November 3 election, denying the Republican a sixth term. NBC News projections showed Jackson leading Collins 52.6 percent to 47.3 percent when she reportedly called to concede. “I called Troy Jackson tonight to congratulate him and to assure him that my staff and I will work to ensure a smooth transition,” Collins stated, according to Punchbowl News senior congressional reporter Andrew Desiderio. 

Democrats backed Jackson after their initial candidate, Graham Platner, who faced scrutiny over a Nazi tattoo, exited the race following allegations of sexual misconduct and rape. Jackson’s campaign also faced scrutiny over allegations that his longtime partner is his second cousin.

Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-WV), who supported Collins’ reelection campaign, argued during an October appearance on NewsNation’s The Hill that Jackson’s decision to campaign alongside prominent progressives reflected how he would govern. “Bernie and AOC and Elizabeth, I doubt they ever knew the other opponent, Susan’s opponent, up there. And they come from the far left of the Democratic Party,” Manchin said, adding that the people a candidate chooses to campaign alongside indicate “where you’re going to go and how you’re going to vote and represent your state.”

news.title: Houston in talks to host Essence Fest after New Orleans departure
news.text:
The city of Houston, Texas, says it is in talks to host the Essence Festival of Culture, after festival organizers announced this week that the annual event was leaving its longtime host city of New Orleans after more than 30 years.

"With confirmation this week that the event is leaving New Orleans, we can confirm that Houston has been in direct talks with Sundial Media Group, the owner of Essence, to bring the festival to our city," Houston Mayor John Whitmire said Wednesday in a joint statement with Houston First Corporation President and CEO Michael Heckman. "Those discussions have accelerated significantly in recent weeks."

VIDEO: 2025 Essence Festival spotlights Disney, Hulu, and Nat Geo in New Orleans 

The mayor said his team is "encouraged by the possibilities" of what Essence Festival would look like if it was brought to Texas and touted Houston's "rich Black cultural heritage."

The organizers of Essence Festival, which takes places every year over the Fourth of July weekend, previously announced in a letter Tuesday that it was starting "a new chapter beyond New Orleans in 2027" and thanked festival participants and the Crescent City for its hospitality.

In a statement shared with ABC News on Wednesday, a spokesperson for Essence said in part, "We know the people of New Orleans are processing this news. After 32 years, we did not take this decision lightly, but we needed to do what was in the best interest of the community."

The spokesperson said despite the festival generating "more than $300 million in economic impact" for New Orleans, "it has to keep growing for the community it serves." 

"We have been heartened by the overwhelming interest from cities across the country to host the festival's legacy and its future," they added. "We are excited about what is ahead and committed to continuing to make ESSENCE the biggest, most joyful festival for Black culture in the world, and can't wait to share our 2027 Festival plans. To New Orleans: thank you for 32 years."

According to NOLA.com, the online news website for The Times-Picayune, the decision to part ways came after months of failed long-term contract negotiations to keep the festival in the city. The city's previous seven-year contract expired earlier this fall, according to the outlet.

Thousands have since commented on the festival's announcement on Instagram, with several people lamenting the move.

"People don't come to Essence fest just for the festivals they come for the City of New Orleans culture as well," one person commented in part. "Food, music bourbon street. It gives visitors something to do before the concerts."

Another person wrote, "If we can't go to Nola for Essence, where can you go?! It's upsetting me and my homegirls."

Following the festival's announcement, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno announced in an Instagram video that another "world-class" festival celebrating Black culture will take its place next year.

"Ultimately, we are working to team up with some of this country's top Black producers to essentially bring in a festival that one, realizes how important it is to be in the city of New Orleans, and that the city of New Orleans itself is a draw, but also one that will be able to bring in top talent to perform for you, but also to recognize the amount of talent that we have right here in the city of New Orleans with amazing musicians and artists," Moreno said.

Moreno teased another announcement, coming Dec. 9, that will provide more details and reveal what the new festival will be.

"The festival that we'll be bringing to you will also work to do activations not just in downtown New Orleans, but across the city, from New Orleans East to downtown New Orleans to Algiers," Moreno continued. "And then, of course, we need to make sure that there's widespread benefit for our local businesses, particularly our local Black businesses, when it comes to this festival. And so that's the other piece that we're building as well."

The Essence Festival has drawn celebrities, musicians, superstars and politicians to its celebrations over the years, from former Vice President Kamala Harris and former first lady Michelle Obama to Grammy-winning singer Miguel.

The 2026 Essence Festival took place this past July at the New Orleans Ernest N. Morial Convention Center and the Caesars Superdome and featured performers including Brandy, Monica, Kehlani, Latto, Cardi B., T.I., Patti LaBelle, Public Enemy, and George Clinton and Parliament-Funkadelic.

The festival concluded with an Aaliyah tribute performance curated by Missy Elliott, with performances from Mýa, Normani, Chlöe and more.

ABC News has reached out to Mayor Moreno's office for comment.
news.summary: The Essence Festival of Culture is leaving its longtime home of New Orleans after more than 30 years.

news.title: Maddow says Democrats can abolish Electoral College if they 'swing for the fences'
news.text: MS NOW host Rachel Maddow said during an interview on Saturday that getting rid of the Electoral College was "doable" for Democrats if they "swing for the fences." MS NOW's Jacob Soboroff asked Maddow about her thoughts on Democrats getting rid of the system, which has received criticism after the last two Republican presidents won their first elections despite losing the national popular vote. "My whole life, it has been this kind of theoretical, you know, this hypothetical math problem. You know, if ever enough states to speak for 270 electoral votes all got into this agreement, then it would go into effect, and it always just seems so pie in the sky," she said. GOP WIPEOUT GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE AS DEMS QUIETLY SCORE ANOTHER MAJOR WIN WITH BIG RAMIFICATIONS Maddow said she felt it was doable for the Democrats after speaking with Ben Wikler, a Democratic advocate for eliminating the Electoral College. Soboroff and Maddow said that Democrats could use the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement that makes it so a state will award all of their electoral votes to whichever presidential candidate wins the overall national popular vote — regardless of who actually won the vote inside that individual state. GAVIN NEWSOM EXPRESSES 'OPENNESS' TO PACKING SCOTUS, CALLS ELECTORAL COLLEGE SYSTEM 'PERVERTED' Eighteen states have signed the compact, in addition to Washington, D.C., which means the compact has 222 electoral votes pledged to it — 48 short of the 270 needed to take effect. However, Democrats now control the governor’s office and both chambers of the state legislatures in the swing states of Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Nevada. Those legislatures' combined 50 electoral votes would push the compact to 272 and activate it should they vote to sign the compact. PROGRESSIVES UNVEIL $25 MINIMUM WAGE PUSH TO SOLVE AFFORDABILITY CRISIS DESPITE ECONOMIST INFLATION WARNING "There are enough Democratic states right now who have a Democratic trifecta — governor and the full legislature — that puts you way over 270 if they all decided to do it, and you don't need very many states to act right now for that to be operative," Maddow said. "It's doable. I mean, raising the minimum wage is doable. Getting rid of the Electoral College is doable, age limits for Supreme Court justices might be doable. I mean, the Democrats have big majorities and if they decide to swing for the fences, they could do a lot right now." We need more justices on the Supreme Court so that we can have a court that actually reinforces the spirit and principles behind the Constitution of the United States," Harris told podcast host Keke Palmer. "I believe that we should be pushing for what is possible around changing the Electoral College. Right?" she added. Lise Hand: Trump hates women, and the media, and especially women in the media

Trump threw his power in the tech world around this week with the rehiring of Jensen Huang – and managed to be vulgar along the way.

7.01pm, 25 Nov 2026

Share options

IT’S A NAILED-ON racing certainty that if perchance some Irish business bigwig had hurriedly exited from his top job for – shall we say – ‘conduct unbecoming’, only to be suddenly and inexplicably reinstated, the Taoiseach of the day would not celebrate by posting an AI-generated meme of an event at which someone died violently, featuring the triumphant bigwig holding aloft a bra.

If such a repulsive and bizarre image did pop up in a Taoiseach’s social media feed, the immediate assumption would be that his account had been hacked. And then, upon discovering that it had indeed been created by our head of government, the tumbrils would rumble up Merrion Street and the (metaphorical) head would be promptly demanded. In jig time he would be an ex-Taoiseach who, to quote Monty Python, had now expired and gone to join the choir invisible.

But just such a meme, for anyone who snatched forty winks on Monday and missed an entire U.S. news cycle, was posted by a jubilant President Trump a short time after the shock announcement that Jensen Huang was returning to his position as CEO of Nvidia.

The fake image of Jensen Huang that was shared by TrumpDonald Trump / Truth Social

Donald Trump / Truth Social / Truth Social

To briefly summarise the chaos: Huang resigned on 12 November after revelations that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy who’d routed embargoed Nvidia chips to Chinese AI companies. Reportedly Huang also had undisclosed relationships with two of his employees, including a vice president who reported directly to him. Cue stock market panic, plunging shares amid tech bro terror that the whole AI malarkey could also shortly do an ex-parrot and start pining for the fjords. So Trump personally put the arm on Nvidia’s board and hey presto Huang was back with a, well, bang.

Not long after the bombshell announcement that the prodigal multibillionaire had returned, the president took to Truth Social, posting an AI slop version of the iconic ‘fight, fight, fight’ image taken in the immediate aftermath of the assassination attempt on him during a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania in 2026. Instead, it was Huang’s face streaked with blood, and in his raised fist was a scarlet-coloured bra.

There was immediate outrage. Some people were aghast, pointing out that one person had been killed that day and that a second victim who had sustained serious injuries in the shooting died just two months ago in September. There was also outrage and unease on Capitol Hill where not everybody was buying into the “move along, nothing spy-related to see here” nonchalance emanating from the White House who were insisting that Huang’s credibility is not only intact but enhanced, even, and that everything’s tickety-boo.

Trump and Jesen Huang at the White House in April 2025.Ken Cedeno / UPI via Alamy

Ken Cedeno / UPI via Alamy / UPI via Alamy

Trump, naturally, didn’t give a monkey’s – au contraire. He and the tech bros and the stock market were immediately en fête. Taking credit for Houdini Huang during a phone call to CNBC, the president exulted: “I think he’s gonna start off at an almost higher level. He’s apologised for the indiscretion. Sex sells, fellas.”

Sex sells, fellas.

Even by the short-fingered vulgarian’s usual low standards, this was grim. The priority was to restart the stuttering stock market gravy-train – a vehicle upon which Nvidia shareholder Trump himself is firmly on board, reportedly making $15m (€13.71 million) in the trillion-bucks rebound. Everything else was irrelevant, collateral damage, useful material for a crudely insulting meme.

Advertisement

But it also served as a grim reminder of just how normalised casual sexism and misogyny have become in Donald Trump’s America – granted, it’s deeply ingrained everywhere, but the US is the poster boy for it.

The fact that the Nvidia CEO has reportedly conducted affairs with two colleagues, not to mention his alleged romance with a woman who has had contact with members of Chinese intelligence, is regarded as a nothingburger is stark – hey, what’s the point of being a bigwig if you can’t enjoy the perks of the job, eh? Ol’ Jensen is some man for one man, here’s a meme to celebrate the return of the horndog, oh wait, let’s stick in a bra!

The White House frat house

The disrespect of women and the degradation of their rights was bad enough in Trump’s first term, but it has worsened this second time around.

The White House is a frat house, doused in eau de machismo and peopled with preposterous figures who have the president’s ear, such as the so-called ‘Secretary of War’ Pete Hegseth who wants women out of the military and who basked in the praise of his boss for doing a “great job” with his anti-DEI drive in getting rid of “woke” generals.

Vice-president JD Vance may have been earmarked for his gig when he sneered during a 2021 interview on Fox News that the U.S. was being run by “a bunch of childless cat ladies who are miserable at their own lives and the choices that they’ve made,” specifically naming Kamala Harris, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Pete Buttigieg, a gay man.

And where to begin with Trump’s on-again-off-again BFF, the planet’s richest man, Elon Musk, who arrived into the White House to take up a key position, trailing multiple sexual misconduct allegations in his wake and pursuing a creepy mission to seed the planet with his offspring (at least 14, to date).

Attacks on female journalists

The Commander-in-Chief, unshackled from the constraints of having to run for office again, routinely attacks journalists who have the audacity to ask what he sees as impertinent questions, which are in fact extremely pertinent – and he’s noticeably more vicious when a woman is in the firing-line, as this sample of recent interactions at press gaggles shows all-too clearly.

To CNN’s Kaitlin Collins: “CNN is a very corrupt organisation with a corrupt reporter standing right there, never smiles, a young beautiful woman never smiles, I see her standing there with hatred in her eyes.”

To CNN’s Kristen Holmes: “No, CNN poll numbers are fake, and your whole outfit is fake, and so are you.”

To Bloomberg’s Catherine Lucey : “Quiet. Quiet, piggy.”

CBS News / YouTube

To ABC’s Mary Bruce: “It’s your attitude. I think you are a terrible reporter. It’s the way you ask these questions… a horrible, insubordinate question.”

To NBC’s Yamiche Alcindor, who is Black: “I know you don’t see dirt, but if you take a look at the White House, you’d never notice broken windows, obviously, from where you come… But we had 18 broken windows.”

Temple Bar nearly became a big bus station. Are we better off it didn't?

A blackout in a foreign city made me realise I'd be utterly unprepared for a national emergency

To CNN’s Kristen Holmes: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive. It’s quite troubling.”

To NBC’s Monica Alba: ““Quiet! You’re a horrible little reporter, aren’t you?”

Commenting on a question by ABC’s Karen Travers: “I had one woman from ‘ABC Fake News’, one of the worst of all… this woman starts screaming.

I recognise her immediately – not a particularly attractive person, inside or out.

“In fact, I just am amazed that these people can be reporters or anchors. She’s screaming. She’s a nasty person.”

On NYT’s Maggie Haberman: “Maggot Hagerman, the Fake Reporter from The Failing New York Times, an unattractive person both inside and out, and who knows less about me than most reporters on the beat (She’s a SCAMMER!).”

Such sexist bullying rarely causes a ripple anymore. It’s shrugged off. Just Trump being Trump.

CNN / YouTube

The glass cliff

His anger towards women is always ready to bubble over; despite various male members of his inner circle such as FBI director Kash Patel, Robert Kennedy Jr. and Hegseth becoming embroiled in various controversies and bad calls, the figures being ejected through the Oval Office’s swing doors are almost all female. And most have been replaced by men.

Most recently, his chief of staff Susan Wiles was replaced by hard-right zealot Stephen Miller, and also this term Trump has fired or pushed out at least half a dozen top women including Attorney General Pam Bondi, Labour Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, and White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia. (Zacharia announced the departure of Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle from the White House podium – the only news she would share, it turned out – a mere three days before she too was handed her P45.) Moreover, Zacharia was replacing Karoline Leavitt who had ceded the position of faithful presidential guard dog to the Stepford Printer, Trump’s deeply weird executive assistant Natalie Harp.

Trump now floats in a dangerous bubble of he-men and yes-men and subordinate women who know their place. In his social milieu, he’s surrounded by women who have literally moulded themselves into his preferred aesthetic of ‘Mar-A-Lago face’, best described as high, dark, arched brows; cartoonishly inflated lips; skin frozen and pulled tautly over multiple syringes’ worth of filler; and barely open eyes that appear to have been pulled sideways and up. Mere coincidence? A quick search for images of philanthropist Susan Dell, Callista Gingrich, wife of Newt Gingrich, far-right activist Laura Loomer and the above-mentioned Kimberly Guilfoyle, would suggest otherwise.

All of it makes for a depressing vista.

But maybe there’s a sliver of hope – as a result of the midterm Blue tsunami, the Democrats will have over 100 women serving in Congress for the first time and perhaps they can begin to recalibrate the gender power imbalance.

But judging by Huang’s unsettling Houdini act, it looks like the broligarchy won’t cede ground without a fight, fight, fight.

news.title: 'The View' Co-Host Ana Navarro Slams Democrats Who Insist Party Must Nominate a White Man in 2028
news.text:
Ana Navarro erupted in an expletive-filled rant over Democrats pushing for a white male to be top of the presidential ticket in 2028, RadarOnline.com can reveal. 

The 54-year-old The View panelist noted that some within the party want to go that route after both Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris suffered losses to Donald Trump in 2016 and 2024. However, Joe Biden managed to topple the tycoon in the 2020 race for the White House.Ana Navarro Attempts to Take Break From 'Insanity of Our Political World'The CNN political pundit opened the Monday, November 23, episode of her Bleep! With Ana Navarro podcast by promising she'd lay off the heavy political talk that usually dominates the program. 

"This week is Thanksgiving, so I wanted to take a break from the dysfunction and insanity of our political world, and I wanted us to have a little fun," she told viewers while introducing her guests, actor-comedians Anthony Anderson and Cedric the Entertainer.

But Navarro then turned to the 2028 presidential race and said some people in the Democratic Party want a "white man" to run against the GOP's nominee for the White House.Ana Navarro Thinks Dems Are 'Scarred' From Kamala Harris and Hillary Clinton's Losses to Trump"You know, there's all this talk of whether Kamala Harris should run again or should not run again. And I hear people saying, 'No, this time we've got to nominate a white man,' because I think people are scarred, are scarred from the fact that two very qualified women, Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris, lost against the most unqualified human being that has ever set foot in the Oval Office," Navarro huffed, referring to the longtime career politicians' losses to real estate mogul Trump. 

"But it p----- me off to hear that said. And I'm hearing it from women, and I'm hearing it from Black women, and I'm hearing it from feminist women and liberal women who supported Kamala, who supported Hillary, because again, I think people are scarred," she explained.'We've Got to Keep Trying'Anderson asked Navarro, "Do you honestly think that the world that we live in here in the United States, do you think they are willing to have a female in the most powerful chair in the world? Do you think we're willing to do that?"

"I don't know. But I think we've got to keep trying," the political commentator fired back. "I mean, I don't want to tell little Black girls and little brown girls that they are out of the game from the start just because of the color of their skin or their gender. So, if they're qualified, h--- yes."Kamala Harris' Earliest Political Backer Urging Her Not to Run in 2028Despite her 2024 defeat to Trump, Harris, 62, is reportedly weighing another White House bid in 2028. But one of her earliest political backers has urged the former vice president to abandon her comeback dreams, and his objections have nothing to do with her being a woman.

"I'm sorry that she even thinks about running for president. I don't want her to run," California political kingpin and Harris ex-boyfriend Willie Brown told The Red Letter's Tara Palmeri on November 23, but said it has nothing to do with her qualifications since "She’s reached the highest electoral level for any woman in America."

Brown, 92, took aim at Harris' struggles to connect with voters during the 2024 presidential election, suggesting her "word salads" left Americans scratching their heads over where she actually stood on key issues.

"She's not a communicator," he declared. "No Baptist preacher flavor in her soul."

news.title: Influencers Behaving Badly at No 10? Burnham could have worse problems | Emma Brockes
news.text:
These are dangerous times to be a prime minister. So it is perhaps reassuring that the trouble into which Andy Burnham barrelled this week is so old school as to be almost soothing. Four months into his premiership, Burnham has arrived early at that rite of passage: the catastrophic attempt to engage with popular culture and subsequent category-5 storm in a teacup. After footage emerged of Influencers Behaving Badly at Downing Street, Burnham, in my view, has come out of the whole thing in surprisingly good shape.

To recap: earlier this month, Burnham held a reception for social media influencers, one of whom, Luke Hamnett, was permitted to film himself doing the Hugh Grant dance from Love Actually before sitting down to interview the prime minister. Meanwhile, self-described “presenter, podcaster, idiot” Max Balegde filmed himself outside the door of No 10 miming what, in the words of the Daily Mail as it geared up to go the full Judge Pickles, “appeared to be a viral meme song”. These words were “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets”, which, as the Telegraph took a breath from its own meltdown to explain, turns on “a Jamaican profanity popularised online”.

If you can absorb any of these details without laughing like a drain, you are a more serious person than me. But in any case, it isn’t the content so much as what the influencers represent that has launched Burnham’s opponents into orbit. I’m not familiar with the line “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets”, but for those of us with young children, it is instantly recognisable as the latest contribution to the “skibidi toilet” meme tradition of conjoining rude words a 10-year-old would find funny and putting them on endless repeat. This would be more embarrassing for Burnham were it not for one fact: between them, Balegde and Hamnett have more than six million followers across Instagram and TikTok, substantially more than the Daily Telegraph. We can be confident the average age of those followers is not 61.

Data as provoking as this obviously calls for a full-throated overreaction, and Kemi Badenoch didn’t disappoint. On Tuesday, the Tory leader requested an apology from the prime minister for turning No 10 into “his personal studio to carry out these silly TikToks”. All right, grandma! She went on to point out that, assuming Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping had watched these videos, enemies of the UK would “see that our prime minister is not a serious man and they will think we are not a serious country”. I have to say this was my favourite part of the whole saga, evoking as it did the tail lights of a ship that sailed decades ago when we elected a former head of communications at Carlton TV, David Cameron, followed by fake model-bus enthusiast Boris Johnson and highly perishable Liz Truss to the top job in this very serious nation. Good one, Kemi!

Meanwhile, Burnham himself had to put a certain amount of damage limitation into place. While it stopped short of an apology, it did involve a spokesperson calling the Balegde video “clearly not acceptable” and it being removed from the influencer’s account. And just when you thought it couldn’t get any better, up popped Nigel Farage with what read to me like a very ambivalent condemnation, indicating that he too – and it pains me to say this, since it plays in his favour – had found the whole thing hilarious. “I wouldn’t let them behave quite the way that it happened,” he said when asked if, were he prime minister, he’d invite influencers to Downing Street. “It showed a slight lack of respect for the place and for the office and was really very inappropriate indeed.” Lot of qualifiers in that statement, Nigel; we can hear you laughing from here.

For the rest of us, I suspect Influencergate has provided a brief, luminous break from real news. If it has a vibe of Michael Crawford on runaway skates flying down a hill – to cite a reference followers of Hamnett and Balegde probably won’t get – there is also a serious part: it’s entirely sensible for Burnham to court influencers in an effort to engage young people in politics. As a cautionary tale, we might look to the US and the disastrous decision made by Kamala Harris during the last presidential election not to appear on Joe Rogan’s podcast and talk to parts of the country old media can’t reach.

In Burnham’s case, the charge isn’t that he sucked up to political enemies, but rather that he engaged in a puff piece at the expense of more robust political interviews. (Hamnett opened the encounter with the remark: “I’m so proud you’re prime minister”, and it got friendlier from there.) And yet there’s no indication the prime minister will stop talking to higher-end hacks and, for my money, he has come out on top – partly for the sheer entertainment value of watching the Tories try to grab the moral high ground and partly because of a quality in Burnham himself.

At the top of Hamnett’s interview, with a bloody great neon sign advertising his podcast jammed into the Downing Street fireplace and the influencer sitting there in slacks, (Prada!) trainers and a daffy look, you can see something happening in Burnham’s expression. It advances, slowly, from affable, to sheepish, to what looks to me like an “oh, God” moment when he understands there’s a good chance all this nonsense will go south. Ironically, it’s the thing politicians dream of; an instant in which the audience, with a smile, thinks we can all relate to that.

 Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

news.title: Democrats to include creators and influencers to maximize viewership for presidential primary debates
news.text: The Democratic Party announced on Monday that its upcoming presidential primary debate process will include "creators and influencers," sparking excitement on the left and mockery from conservatives. The Democrats announced 12 debates starting in June 2027, and candidates must denounce dark money spending in the primary in order to access the debate stage. The DNC added that it will "seek to maximize the viewership of the debates" by incorporating content creators and influencers, as many popular online personalities draw massive audiences. Ben Tyson, co-founder of Good Fight Political, a Democratic campaign firm, said it’s a "great step" by the DNC to include creators and influencers when determining the 2028 presidential nominee. "I'm excited to see them take steps to broaden and modernize the media reach of the upcoming primary debates. It's still too early to know for sure what this will look like exactly, but the big picture is more important than the details to me. Generating an effective narrative in today's media ecosystem requires a recognition of the connectivity between legacy and social media, which is exactly what this effort seems primed to accomplish," Tyson told Fox News Digital. HASAN PIKER MAKES AOC HIS 2028 PICK FOR PRESIDENT, SAYS IT'S 'NOT EVEN A QUESTION’ It’s unclear which creators and influencers will be involved, but far-left streamer Hasan Piker, as well as far-left journalists Mehdi Hasan and Ryan Grim, have each expressed interest. Tyson cited Reuters Institute's 2026 Digital News Report that found 77% of adults globally watch online news videos every week, largely on platforms like YouTube, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook. "Social media is the new home of legacy press content, and for a narrative to truly penetrate to voters, it requires harnessing traditional press to write about it, and then getting creators and everyday users need to share and promote it," Tyson said. "So, whether it ends up being questions from local creators and influencers, bringing them into the audience, or all the way to having creator partnerships in moderating and hosting debates, I'm glad to see the DNC is meeting the moment and bringing a modern media approach to the upcoming presidential primary," Tyson continued. Tyson said the DNC completely revamped its approach to social media for the 2026 campaign, generating more than 13 billion views from thousands of posts, reaching five times as many users as in 2024, and building a clip-sharing network of more than 700 creators, according to the party’s post-election recap. "This looks like another positive step to continue building on that work," Tyson said. "From our perspective, we actively encourage the campaigns we work with to include clipping and creator outreach as fundamentals in their media toolkits, including working with real-life streamers to try to proactively generate this earned media feedback loop that we see in the most prominent campaigns across the country." INSIDE HASAN PIKER’S RADICAL VIEWS ON AMERICA, ISRAEL AND SOCIALISM Heritage Action media fellow Tim Young, who has over 1.1 million followers on X alone, feels Democrats will botch the primary process if social media influencers are too involved. "The last few times Democrats went hard in on influencers, we saw a woman famous for taking a bath in a bathtub full of Froot Loops interview Barack Obama, we saw a trans woman topless on the White House lawn, and we saw an interesting intern in a dress with long fingernails," Young told Fox News Digital. "I can only imagine the lack of seriousness that the Democrat Party will have in their debate schedule," Young continued. "Especially when the last time there was a primary election, their nominee, Vice President Kamala Harris, didn’t receive a single vote on her pathway to ‘victory.’" Indeed, GloZell Green was widely known for a "Froot Loop Challenge" when she interviewed then-President Obama in 2015, transgender content creator Rose Montoya was banned from White House events after posing topless on the South Lawn during a Pride Month event hosted by then-President Joe Biden, and Gen Z influencer Benito Skinner promoted the COVID-19 vaccine alongside former White House press secretary Jen Psaki. HASAN PIKER IS BECOMING THE 'FACE OF THE PROGRESSIVE MOVEMENT,' FORMER DEMOCRATIC OPERATIVE WARNS Despite backlash to all three stunts, Young doesn’t expect Democrats to pivot on the heels of the blue tsunami that occurred during the midterm elections. "Their current strategy wins, so get ready for whatever the unserious circus may be," Young said. Former DNI chief of staff Alexa Henning doesn’t anticipate the Democrats' social media approach to be particularly successful, either. "Democrats looking at 2024 and deciding they need more influencers is what happens when everyone in the strategy meeting wants an invitation to the same parties. It failed then, it’ll fail again," Henning told Fox News Digital. news.title: ROOKE: Gov. Sanders Can’t Lead GOP With Her Massive Blind Spot On Young Men
news.text:
Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders seems to be vying for power within the Republican Party, but she can’t even find a way out of the mess she created. 

In September, Sanders released a midterm ad painting young white men as the face of the welfare state. She then appeared on screen telling voters they shouldn’t have to subsidize healthy adults who “just choose not to work.” Almost instantly, the ad was denounced as out of touch with reality and disrespectful towards young, white men who are a critical voting bloc for Republicans. Like most elected officials, she refused to see reason, defending the ad, claiming that any criticism was connected to her welfare work requirement and not the terrible way she painted young men. 

Sanders still seems not to have absorbed the central lesson of the 2026 midterms or the backlash of her welfare ad. In a Sunday interview with the Daily Signal, Sanders was asked about the contentious ad. She dismissed the criticisms, immediately pivoting to parroting her line about how “able-bodied adults” shouldn’t receive welfare, framing the condemnation as something that “seems to go against everything that conservatives have been pushing for.”

She’s had months and a terrible GOP election night to reflect on her original response, as well as ample time to decide how she’d respond if a journalist asked her about it. She, of course, knows that the critics objected to the specific choice of casting a young white male gamer as the representative face of welfare dependency. And yet she continues to treat the entire episode as a fight over work requirements and not the actual issue. The criticism against her did not reject her policy of requiring work or training to access welfare. By refusing to acknowledge this was a rejection of her portrayal of young men, Sanders signals to her gala-going friends that she’s still a “safe” Republican. 

“Don’t worry, friends. I’m not going to talk about anything that truly matters.”

The optics and accuracy of the messaging do not matter to her. It’s of no significance to her that young white men are among the lowest-rate groups on major welfare programs. Nationally and in her home state of Arkansas, participation rates in SNAP and Medicaid are higher among black and Hispanic adults than whites. Yes, it’s accurate to state that white Americans form a majority of caseloads in Arkansas, but that is simply because the state is roughly 70 percent white. The catch is that the rate at which they enroll is still lower. Even more embarrassing for Sanders is the fact that childless young men, especially young white men like the one portrayed in her ad, are actually a small minority of recipients. (Sign up for Mary Rooke’s weekly newsletter here!)

And before you ask why this ad matters so much, it’s important to take a look at just how badly Republicans did with young men during the midterm elections. The same demographic (young men) that delivered decisive support for Republicans in 2024 abandoned them in 2026.

CIRCLE’s analysis of AP VoteCast data found that young men ages 18-29 backed President Donald Trump over former Vice President Kamala Harris 56 percent to 42 percent in 2024. Young white men did so by an even greater margin, supporting Trump 63 percent to Kamala’s 35 percent. That is a decisive shellacking thanks to what could have been a generational voting bloc, but Republicans squandered it. CIRCLE’s analysis of NORC Civic Health and Elections Project data from the 2026 midterms shows young men supporting Democratic House candidates by 22 points. Young white men in particular went from a 28-point Republican advantage to an 11-point Democratic advantage in one election. Not just that, but overall young voter turnout fell off a cliff. 

Now you can’t blame this shift on Sanders’ ad alone. But combine it with Trump breaking his promise not to start new wars and the state of the economy pushing the American Dream farther away from them than ever before, and the election data becomes understandable to any reasonable person watching. However, to Sanders, it seems to have flown over her head once again. 

Days after the midterms, she posted a New York Post headline claiming “shell-shocked Republicans were looking to [her] for the blueprint on how to resurrect the party.” The story praised her 15-point reelection margin, which, to be fair in this election cycle, was impressive. However, it immediately went off the rails, noting her defense of the Iran War. Interestingly, it made no mention of the ad or the collapse among the young male voters, which, of course, means it also didn’t include her plan to win them back. (RELATED: GOP Misreads The Midterms, While Democrats Are Adjusting Their Playbook)

She so desperately wants to be treated as a national model for Republican victory, but she fails the most basic test. No serious observer of the midterm elections is turning to the governor who spent precious political capital demonizing the very voters the GOP needs and refuses to understand her mistake.

news.title: Still Making Headlines! What Past Root 100 Honorees Are Up To Right Now
news.text:
It’s no secret that Black politicians, athletes, leaders and entertainers honored on The Root 100 annual list always make their mark, but the story doesn’t stop there! For 17 years, The Root 100 has celebrated the Black visionaries, cultural icons and changemakers shaping conversations, breaking barriers and influencing generations. 

From award-winning legends like Misty Copeland and groundbreaking journalist Abby Phillip to cultural icons and game-changing leaders like Jasmine Crockett and Al Roker, these trailblazers continued making moves in 2026. Now, we’re checking in on where they are, celebrating the wins, the milestones and moments that keep their names in the conversation.

Abby Phillip Then

Abby Phillip joined The Root 100 in 2025, celebrating her influential journalism and contributions to conversations about politics, power and representation.

Abby Phillip Now

Abby Phillip has continued commanding the political conversation as CNN’s “NewsNight” anchor. In 2026, she also appeared at the Library of Congress National Book Festival, bringing her work on Jesse Jackson and Black political power to readers. Phillip and her husband, Marcus Richardson, welcomed their second child, son Maxwell Elias Richardson, in October following an IVF journey.

Randall Woodfin Then

Birmingham Mayor Randall Woodfin joined The Root 100 in 2018, earning recognition for his leadership and commitment to creating new opportunities for residents of one of America’s most historic Black cities.

Randall Woodfin Now

Randall Woodfin is still putting Birmingham first! In November 2025, the mayor officially began his third term, continuing his work to revitalize the city’s neighborhoods, expand educational opportunities and strengthen economic development. Through initiatives like Birmingham Promise, he’s also keeping his focus on creating pathways to college and careers for the next generation. His mission to build a stronger Birmingham is far from finished!

Misty Copeland Then

Misty Copeland joined The Root 100 celebration in 2023, honoring her groundbreaking career and lasting impact on ballet and Black representation.

Misy Copeland Now

Misty Copeland has never been content with simply breaking barriers; she’s determined to make sure others can walk through them, too. In 2026, the ballet trailblazer added a new distinction to her résumé, joining the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Board of Trustees while continuing her advocacy for greater access to dance.

Jasmine Crockett Then

Texas Rep. Jasmine Crockett hit the Root 100 red carpet in 2024, celebrating her fearless leadership and growing influence in American politics.

Jasmine Crockett Now

The Texas congresswoman spent 2026 keeping the pressure on Washington, championing voting rights and civil rights while continuing to challenge political power with the sharp tongue and fearless approach that have made her a force in the national conversation. Marc Lamont Hill brought his signature blend of journalism, scholarship and cultural commentary to The Root 100, celebrating his influence as an educator, author and outspoken voice in conversations about race, politics and social justice.

Tamron Hall joined The Root 100’s celebration of Black achievement, bringing her celebrated journalism career and commitment to storytelling into the spotlight.

Tamron Hall continues making moves in daytime television! Nikole Hannah-Jones is continuing to shape conversations about race, history and democracy. news.text: Democratic U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff has insisted he has no interest in running for president in 2028, but his commanding reelection in Georgia and rapid rise in national polling have intensified speculation about who could stop him if he changed his mind. Ossoff, 39, defeated Republican Representative Mike Collins by about 18 points this month in a state President Donald Trump carried by roughly 2 points in 2024. His margin, combined with significant gains among Latino voters, men, young voters and white voters without college degrees, has fueled the argument that he could assemble the kind of broad coalition Democrats will need to regain the White House. Polling has reinforced the buzz. In a closed-ended hypothetical Democratic primary matchup conducted by Emerson College after the midterms, Ossoff received 17 percent, narrowly ahead of former Vice President Kamala Harris at 16 percent, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at 15 percent and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 14 percent. But a hypothetical Ossoff candidacy would face intense competition, and two University of Georgia political scientists who spoke to Newsweek pointed particularly to governors with their own records of winning difficult elections. Statewide exit polling showed Ossoff winning 93 percent of Black voters and about two-thirds of Latino voters while making substantial gains compared with Harris' 2024 performance among men, white voters and white voters without college degrees. He won 40 percent of white voters, compared with Harris' 28 percent two years earlier, and 29 percent of non-college-educated white voters, compared with Harris' 18 percent. The 2026 exit polling was conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of major news organizations. The comparisons are not exact because presidential and midterm electorates differ, but they illustrate the breadth of Ossoff's improvement over the party's 2024 performance. Charles S. Bullock III, distinguished university professor of public and international affairs and Richard B. Russell professor of political science at the University of Georgia, told Newsweek that Ossoff also ran roughly 4 to 5 points ahead of other Democrats seeking statewide office and deserved some credit for helping the party elect its first statewide constitutional officers in two decades. Bullock said Ossoff could point to his support for broadly popular policies, including capping monthly insulin costs at $35 and improving maternal health care, while positioning himself as a strong critic of the Trump administration. “A non-ideological candidate who talks about costs, access to healthcare, and disengagement from wars in the Middle East will be more likely to succeed, and Ossoff checks those boxes,” Bullock said. There are vulnerabilities, however. Bullock said Ossoff's questioning of U.S. aid for Israel's military campaign against Iran could appeal to younger voters while causing problems with some older voters. His Southern background and voting record could also create difficulties with the Democratic Party's liberal wing. Jamie L. Carson, athletic professor of public and international affairs in the department of political science at the University of Georgia, cautioned against assuming Ossoff's Georgia coalition would automatically translate nationally. “His victory deserves serious attention,” Carson told Newsweek. “Winning convincingly in a closely divided state demonstrates campaign strength and gives him a credible argument about reaching voters beyond the Democratic base.” But Carson noted that Ossoff was an incumbent running in an unusually favorable environment for Democrats and against a Republican closely aligned with Trump. “The question is how much of that coalition would travel beyond Georgia and survive different political conditions,” Carson said. The Biggest Challengers to an Ossoff Presidential Bid Carson identified Governors Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, Andy Beshear of Kentucky and Gavin Newsom of California as significant potential rivals, alongside Harris. Each would challenge Ossoff differently. Shapiro could make his own electability argument based on his success in Pennsylvania, one of the nation's most important presidential battlegrounds. Beshear could pose an even more direct challenge to Ossoff's crossover appeal as a Democrat who has won statewide in heavily Republican Kentucky. Newsom brings substantial national visibility and a prominent role opposing Trump, while Harris could enter with enormous name recognition, established Democratic relationships and experience as both vice president and the party's 2024 presidential nominee. The governors would also offer executive experience that Ossoff, as a senator, does not have. “Ossoff would have an appealing story to tell, but he would need to establish what distinguishes him from other Democrats who also claim they can win difficult elections and effectively challenge Republicans,” Carson said. Bullock's analysis points particularly toward candidates capable of occupying Ossoff's own political territory. “A potential winning candidate would be very similar to Ossoff, such as Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear,” Bullock said. “Gretchen Whitmer might also be a problem for an Ossoff candidacy.” That could make Beshear especially significant. Rather than challenging Ossoff primarily from the ideological left or through national celebrity, he could compete directly on one of Ossoff's central potential selling points: winning voters in territory that normally favors Republicans. Could Raphael Warnock Complicate an Ossoff Run? Ossoff could theoretically also face competition much closer to home from fellow Georgia Senator Raphael Warnock. Both Carson and Bullock said they consider a simultaneous presidential run by Georgia's two Democratic senators unlikely. Carson said the pair would compete for overlapping Georgia donors, endorsements and organizational support, even though their political styles and potential national constituencies differ. Their electoral calendars also create different incentives. Ossoff has just won another six-year Senate term, while Warnock faces reelection in 2028. If both entered the contest, Bullock said, they would split the Georgia Democratic Party. He argued that Warnock could have an advantage because Black voters make up a large share of Georgia's Democratic primary electorate and South Carolina, where Black Democrats have long wielded significant influence in the nominating process, will vote first. The Democratic voting calendar could otherwise work to Ossoff's advantage. South Carolina will be followed by Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia, giving Black and Latino voters substantial influence in the opening contests. Those are constituencies that formed important parts of Ossoff's winning coalition in Georgia. Which Democrats Would Challenge Ossoff From a Different Lane? Early polling makes it difficult to dismiss Ocasio-Cortez, Buttigieg or Harris. Organizers have been encouraging Ocasio-Cortez to enter the race, while allies of Buttigieg have launched a grassroots effort aimed at persuading him to mount another White House campaign. But those candidates could appeal to different constituencies rather than directly challenging the electoral argument Ossoff would likely make. A progressive candidacy could attack Ossoff from the left on issues including healthcare and immigration. Ossoff has faced progressive criticism for supporting the Republican-backed Laken Riley Act and not embracing Medicare for All. Bullock, meanwhile, questioned the potential general-election appeal of two of the best-known prospective contenders. “Gavin Newsom would struggle to win Georgia or North Carolina or Texas,” he said. “Kamala Harris, if she should try a comeback, would also have difficulty succeeding on what I call the southern path to the White House.” That differs somewhat from Carson's assessment of Newsom and Harris as formidable potential primary competitors. The distinction matters: A candidate can pose a serious threat to Ossoff in the Democratic nominating contest without necessarily matching his potential argument about winning Southern or swing-state voters in November. Where the 2028 Democratic Race Stands Today For now, the biggest obstacle to an Ossoff presidential campaign may be Ossoff himself. “I have zero interest in running for president,” Ossoff said during an October Senate debate. “I'm not running for president. I'm running for reelection to the Senate.” Carson said that denial should be taken seriously, even though politicians have changed their minds about presidential campaigns before. More important than speculation, he said, will be evidence of an actual national organization developing around Ossoff, including donors, experienced staff, endorsements, fundraising and activity in early primary states. “The central question is whether attention translates into an organization capable of competing nationally,” Carson said. “A prospective candidate also needs a clear rationale for running: what would an Ossoff presidency offer that voters could not get from the other candidates?” The Democratic field remains hypothetical, with no major candidate formally in the race, even as the party begins constructing the machinery for what could become a sprawling primary. Twelve sanctioned Democratic debates are planned from June 2027 to March 2028, with the earliest events potentially accommodating as many as 20 candidates under the framework announced by the Democratic National Committee. That leaves Ossoff plenty of time to decide whether his Georgia victory represents the beginning of a presidential campaign or simply another step in a political career that, at 39, could provide multiple future opportunities to seek the White House. 12:16:12 PM Eastern

[Cuts to video]

12:20:17 PM Eastern

RAJU: So, while this will come up in the president -- in the presidential campaign, maybe not in the primary, you will probably hear some of these attacks reprised in a general election. The voters' views are mixed more on this issue.

12:22:07 PM Eastern

RAJU: Yeah. news.title: Congress is about to have 4 times as many DSA members. Who they are
news.text:
The midterm blue wave was largely won in swing districts by moderate candidates backed by independent voters. But progressives and democratic socialists were also elected in more liberal districts across the country, adding to a growing coalition on Capitol Hill.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, and Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York, and Rashida Tlaib, D-Michigan, are the only democratic socialists already on Capitol Hill. But after winning on Nov. 3, at least six members of the Democratic Socialists of America and three progressives somewhat aligned with their movement will join the House of Representatives.

While Ocasio-Cortez and Tlaib belong to the controversial Democratic Socialists of America organization, Sanders is not a member, though he identifies as a democratic socialist.

The DSA members joining the House

The DSA members headed to Congress in January are Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, and Angela Gonzales-Torres of California.

Valdez, Rabb, and McKinney bring political experience, having served as state legislators. Valdez first won office in 2024 and McKinney in 2023. Rabb has the most experience, having served in the Pennsylvania House since 2017 and previously worked as a legislative aide for former Sen. Carol Moseley Braun, D-Illinois.

Avila Chevalier, Kiros and Gonzales-Torres are political newcomers who won their first bids for office, though each has experience in community advocacy and grassroots organizations in their cities.

Kiros, the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress, is the youngest at 29. Rabb, 56, is the only one over 40. The group is also racially and ethnically diverse, with Black, Dominican, Ethiopian, Puerto Rican, and Mexican backgrounds represented.

Avila Chevalier and Kiros both drew national attention during their campaigns for their outspoken advocacy for Palestinians. In June, CNN's investigative KFile team reported that Avila Chevalier had deleted social media posts calling for abolishing police and prisons and one post that directed explicit language toward former Vice President Kamala Harris.

Another incoming progressive House member is New York's Brad Lander, who voted for Jeffries as leader. He was previously a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, but left the organization after it promoted a rally in New York City days after the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack in Israel, at which some participants defended the attack. Avila Chevalier attended the same rally.

Midterm elections: From LA to NYC, democratic socialists move on City Hall

None of those seven members flipped any of the Democrats' 45 new seats. Instead, they come from seats already held by Democrats, some ousting current members in the primaries and others running in retired members' seats.

Ohio's Brian Poindexter, an ironworker who campaigned as a working-class populist, will join the House of Representatives after beating scandal-tarred Republican Rep. Max Miller. Poindexter was endorsed by the Congressional Progressive Caucus and Sanders, but he has called himself a capitalist and also had an endorsement from the moderate Blue Dog Democratic group.

There are many other progressive Democrats in the House, including Reps. Pramila Jayapal from Washington, Ro Khanna of California, Greg Casar from Texas, Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, and Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts who do not belong to the DSA or identify as socialists.

Tensions with Jeffries

Seven incoming progressive and democratic socialist representatives-elect issued a joint statement Nov. 18 opposing the selection of Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries as the next speaker of the House, saying they were not convinced he would champion their agenda.

"Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues. We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations," Avila Chevalier, Adam Hamawy, Frederick Haynes, Kiros, McKinney, Rabb and Valdez wrote.

"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no," they wrote.

Hamawy from New Jersey and Haynes from Texas are both progressive member-elects who joined the Nov. 18 statement, but neither identify as democratic socialists. Rep.-elect Don Leonard of Ohio, viewed as an anti-establishment progressive, voted against Jeffries after saying he got threats from top Democrats if he didn't back the party leader.

The announcement follows years of tension between Jeffries and DSA activists in his own backyard. At Avila Chevalier's and Valdez's victory parties on the night of New York's June primary, crowds chanted "you're next" at Jeffries' image on TV screens, meaning the Brooklyn representative could face a primary challenge in 2028.

Jeffries ultimately won the vote among Democratic caucus members by a huge margin, 251-11. With a few races still uncalled or headed to runoffs, USA TODAY's most recent election results put Democrats with at least 258 seats and Republicans at 174, giving Democrats the numbers to pass legislation even without the more progressive faction.

But in some cases, moderate Democrats may defect and leave Jeffries with a narrow enough margin that he needs to keep the left wing of his caucus on board.

An urban phenomenon

Democratic socialism is spreading in major cities. New York City and Seattle elected democratic socialist mayors in 2025, and Los Angeles and Washington, DC, joined them in 2026.

The slate of DSA members represents largely urban areas. Ocasio-Cortez, Avila Chevalier, and Valdez all represent New York City districts. Rabb's Pennsylvania district is in Philadelphia, Gonzales-Torres will represent a Los Angeles district, and Kiros' Colorado district is based in the heart of Denver. McKinney will represent parts of Detroit, while Tlaib represents a neighboring district that also includes parts of the city.

Lander's district is also in New York City, while Hamawy's New Jersey district includes Trenton. Haynes won in Rep. Jasmine Crockett's Texas district, which is anchored in Dallas, after she lost a primary bid for the U.S. Senate. Omar represents Minneapolis, and Jayapal's Washington district includes most of Seattle.

In Ohio, Poindexter won in the state's 7th Congressional District that includes Cleveland suburbs, and Leonard's district includes parts of Columbus.

According to the DSA's election night tracker, the organization's endorsed candidates and ballot proposals had 176 wins to 118 losses across federal, state, and local offices. The wins spanned the country, and statewide office winners came from cities like Tampa, Florida, Louisville, Portland, Oregon, Tuscon, Arizona, Atlanta, and Buffalo, New York. Losses came in Sacramento, California, New Orleans, and Las Vegas.

According to NBC News exit polls from the midterms, 18% of all voters identify as democratic socialists.

In statewide elections, the democratic socialist faction did not win any general elections, despite some impressive performances in primaries. State Rep. Angie Nixon, a DSA member, lost in Florida's Senate race by almost 3 percentage points after her upset primary win over Alex Vindman. She got 50,000 fewer votes than David Jolly, the moderate Democratic nominee for Florida governor.

Earlier in the season, state Rep. Francesca Hong, also a DSA member, narrowly lost in the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary after leading in the polls.

In Michigan and Illinois, Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Juliana Stratton won their primaries, after being seen as more progressive candidates, and ultimately won in the general election. Neither El-Sayed nor Stratton, though, identify as democratic socialists.

Sanders will remain the sole democratic socialist in the Senate.

news.title: Go Local Or Go Home: Can Dems Take ‘State by State’ Doctrine Into 2028?
news.text: The summer of 2025 was rough for Democrats in Washington. Relegated to the minority in both chambers of Congress, they watched, relatively powerless, as President Donald Trump upended longstanding norms. Coming off the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Trump and Republicans appeared intent on flexing further muscle over the left by ordering a redistricting effort in Texas aimed at bolstering their congressional majority. Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries railed against it, but there was little he could do. Democratic California Governor Gavin Newsom, however, offered some pushback. Newsom directed the California legislature to redraw its own maps with Prop 50. The move worked. Democrats flipped all five House seats targeted under the effort, and other Democratic governors and their state legislatures followed suit, helping Democrats to clinch at least 258 House seats, the most they’ve held since 1992. Now that Democrats have clawed back control, however, will their donors continue to see value in investing in state government? “Things like redistricting and judicial appointments and that kind of long-term power building have really been enlightening for Democrats [this cycle],” Meghan Meehan-Draper, executive director of the Democratic Governors Association, told Newsweek. “When you elect a Democratic governor, you’re not just getting someone who's going to do good policy, you’re also electing someone who’s going to build their state party.” That argument was not lost on Democratic donors this cycle as the DGA posted record fundraising numbers on its way to winning 30 governorships, a number not seen by the party since 1993. Democrats last held a majority of America’s governorships in 2010, and during President Barack Obama first midterms, were whipped at the ballot box by what the president called a "shellacking" that caused the left's state power to be decimated. Many Democrats have long viewed Washington as the primary answer to America’s problems and have directed fundraising dollars accordingly, sometimes to their detriment. From Amy McGrath’s $90 million Kentucky Senate loss to Republican Mitch McConnell to Jaime Harrison’s $132 million South Carolina blowout loss to Lindsey Graham, Democrats have a history of spending big on federal power grabs only to come up short and be left wondering how that money could have influenced change elsewhere. This cycle proved different as nine Senate seat flips and 48 House flips coincided with six governor mansion flips and six state legislature flips. But those like Meehan-Draper who work in state politics say the fundraising disparity between federal and state races remains an issue. They also argue that the secret to winning those federal contests in the first place rests on an increased commitment from Democrats in amplifying their stateside political efforts. “Our rationale of investing in all 57 state parties so they can do year-round organizing is so that they are constantly connected to the issues, the voters, and the candidates year-round,” Jane Kleeb, president of the Association of State Democratic Committees (ASDC), told Newsweek. “When we invest in just battleground states and ‘outside infrastructure’—like PACs and independent expenditures—that parachute in and focuses our resources at the national level with more consultants, we lose elections.” As ASDC president, Kleeb was a leading part of the effort undertaken by Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin to push national resources toward state parties, an effort that marked a departure from the DNC’s strategy during Obama’s time in office. Kleeb, who served as executive director of the Young Democrats of America from 2004 to 2007, said during the reelection campaign of President George W. Bush that Democratic operatives began advising donors that “state parties and the DNC were ineffective, outdated organizations.” She said they argued for more outside national infrastructure and a greater focus on battleground states, saying such efforts would concentrate both resources and messaging and yield wins. Under DNC Chair Howard Dean, who served in the position from 2005 to 2009, the DNC remained influential, as Dean’s 50-state investment strategy helped deliver electoral wins similar to the success seen this cycle. However, in 2008, Dean was replaced by now Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia who was tasked with integrating Obama’s campaign apparatus, Organizing for America, into the DNC’s fold. State party funding declined, and in the 2010 midterms, Democrats lost six Senate seats, 63 House seats, six governorships, and 11 legislatures. Kleeb said the problem is that the party became too “top-heavy” and there weren’t enough people meeting voters on the ground where they’re at, fueling perceptions of the party being out of touch with regular Americans. Despite that, the desire to concentrate messaging at the top surfaced again following Vice President Kamala Harris’ loss to Trump. “There was this big mantra coming out of the 2024 election cycle that the Democratic brand is toxic and that we needed a ‘national message,’” Kleeb said. “Every room we went into with donors or operatives or think tank people, they kept on drilling myself and Chair Martin on ‘what is the message?’ Chair Martin and I kept on saying this is not about a national message; this is about each state’s candidate developing a message that resonates with them and their experience, but also what is facing their state and local communities. That really ruffled some feathers.” Martin’s DNC was criticized for its investments, yet the 2026 election surpassed the 2006 election in its number of gains. However, analysis suggested that while most elected offices—up and down the ticket—saw Democratic gains ranging from 19 percent to 33 percent, the number of state senate seats flipped this cycle was an outlier, with Democrats seeing just an 11 percent gain in that type of office. Democrats flipped 20 percent of state house seats, but the lower share of state senate seats proved somewhat costly. Republicans maintain narrow majorities in the Georgia, North Carolina, and Texas state senates, preventing Democratic trifectas and impeding their agenda. Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said that while Democrats are increasingly seeing the value of these races, their party’s donor class lags behind Republicans in enthusiasm. “Republicans have done a really good job over the last decade and a half as they ramped-up Project Red Map in 2010 and really implemented the strategy of recognizing the relationship between state and federal power,” Williams told Newsweek. “Even if the national Republican donor base did not know who these state legislative candidates were, they knew the impact of having power in the states to test and move their agenda, to create the bench for future candidates, to control the redistricting process to win the majority of congressional districts, and they really came out with that strategy.” Trump’s return to the White House has no doubt been characterized by a focus on national politics within the Republican Party, as the president has positioned Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as his likely heirs apparent, drawing attention away from GOP senators and governors. In turn, the GOP has seen a concentration of resources toward Trump and his aligned super PAC, MAGA Inc. It was reported in October that “of the nearly 1.5 million donors who have given on WinRed [the Republican online donor platform] this cycle, 324,000 of them—a bit over 22 percent—have given only to Trump’s groups.” Naturally, the president deployed a significant number of resources this cycle toward maintaining control of Congress, but in an unfavorable environment for the GOP, that allowed Democrats to make a push for major state-level gains. Trump will exit office in 2028, however, and Republican donors demonstrated this cycle with multimillion-dollar investments in places like Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, showing they’re eager to invest in state government, especially ahead of 2030 when the new census results will trigger Congressional redistricting. Nationally prominent governors like Newsom may have been able to draw attention to the influence of state government this cycle. However, if Democrats forget what drove their resistance in the era of Trump 2.0 and shift their focus away from state power, history could repeat itself. If 2026’s wins resembled 2006’s victories, 2030 could see a defeat akin to the losses of 2010 if Democrats forget the importance of state power.
news.summary: Having rediscovered the power of governors and state legislators, Democrats may not need a national message to win big in 2028.
